title: Tech Stocks Slide, Stock Futures Mixed After Sector Sell‑Off – Live CNBC Updates
body:
U.S. equity futures opened Friday on a mixed note after a sharp pull‑back in technology stocks erased much of the week’s gains, leaving the Nasdaq Composite on track for its worst single‑day decline since June. The sell‑off, sparked by growing doubts that the current wave of artificial‑intelligence (AI)‑driven hype may be losing momentum, sent the S&P 500 futures down 0.2 percent while the Dow Jones futures edged slightly higher, underscoring the market’s uneven reaction to the tech‑sector turbulence.

The immediate catalyst was a cascade of price drops among the sector’s heavyweight names, including a near‑5 percent slide in Nvidia Corp., the leading chipmaker that has been a bellwether for AI‑related equities. Alphabet Inc. and Microsoft Corp., both of which have heavily invested in AI infrastructure, also posted modest declines, pulling down the broader Nasdaq index. Analysts note that the rapid rise in AI‑centric valuations over the past few months may have outpaced the pace of tangible earnings growth, prompting investors to reassess risk exposure ahead of the upcoming earnings season.

While the tech slump dominated headlines, other market segments displayed resilience. Financials and consumer staples posted modest gains, buoyed by steady earnings forecasts and a relatively stable macro‑economic backdrop. The Dow‑related futures, which are weighted more heavily toward industrial and energy stocks, managed a slight uptick, reflecting confidence that the broader economy remains on a solid footing despite lingering concerns about inflation and monetary policy. However, the divergence between the Nasdaq and the other major indices highlights a growing bifurcation: growth‑oriented stocks are now more vulnerable to sentiment swings than the traditionally defensive sectors.

The underlying anxiety stems from a confluence of factors beyond pure valuation metrics. Recent comments from senior Federal Reserve officials suggesting that interest‑rate hikes could be prolonged have heightened the cost of capital for high‑growth companies that rely on cheap financing to fund research and development. At the same time, supply‑chain bottlenecks in semiconductor manufacturing have persisted, delaying the rollout of next‑generation AI chips and potentially throttling the revenue pipelines of firms that depend on those products. Moreover, a series of mixed earnings reports from AI‑related firms—some beating expectations, others falling short—have added to the uncertainty about the sector’s near‑term earnings trajectory.

Investors are also watching the policy environment closely. The administration’s push for AI regulation, coupled with heightened scrutiny over data privacy and ethical considerations, could impose new compliance costs on tech companies. While regulatory frameworks are still in their infancy, the prospect of stricter oversight may temper the enthusiasm that has driven speculative inflows into AI stocks this year. In contrast, sectors such as utilities and health care, which are less directly impacted by AI policy, continue to attract risk‑averse capital, reinforcing the current sector rotation.

Looking ahead, market participants will likely gauge the durability of the tech pull‑back by monitoring upcoming earnings releases from key AI players and assessing whether the sector can sustain its growth narrative amid tighter monetary conditions. Analysts suggest that a decisive earnings beat from a marquee name like Nvidia could restore confidence and reignite the rally, while a string of disappointing results could accelerate the shift toward more defensive holdings. As the trading week progresses, the balance between optimism for AI’s long‑term potential and caution over short‑term execution will shape the direction of U.S. equity futures and set the tone for the broader market’s next move.
